reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Follows ingestion of bivalve shellfish that have accumulated saxitoxins from toxic dinoflagellate blooms (red tides)
Symptoms typically begin within minutes to an hour with perioral and facial paraesthesiae and tingling of the extremities
Progresses to ataxia, dysarthria, limb weakness and, in severe cases, ascending flaccid paralysis with respiratory failure
As with other sodium-channel toxins, consciousness is characteristically preserved throughout the paralysis
There is no antidote; management is supportive with airway protection and mechanical ventilation until toxin clearance
Early gastrointestinal decontamination may be considered soon after ingestion in a protected airway
The toxins are heat-stable, so cooking does not make contaminated shellfish safe
reference.pathophysiology: Saxitoxin and related paralytic shellfish toxins are produced by marine dinoflagellates and concentrated in filter-feeding bivalves. After ingestion, the toxins bind voltage-gated sodium channels on excitable membranes, blocking sodium conductance and inhibiting nerve and muscle action potentials. This causes early sensory disturbance followed by progressive flaccid paralysis, including of respiratory muscles, which is the principal life threat. The toxins are heat-stable and are not destroyed by normal cooking, and central nervous system function is relatively spared, so consciousness is retained despite paralysis.
additionalDifferentials: Scombroid poisoning (though this is histaminic rather than paralytic)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on shellfish ingestion and characteristic neurology
Continuous respiratory monitoring and serial forced vital capacity
Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases for ventilatory failure
Electrolytes and baseline bloods to exclude alternative causes
Toxin assay of shellfish or biological samples where available, and public health notification
redFlags: Progressive limb, bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness
Declining respiratory function or oxygen saturation
Rapid symptom onset after a large ingestion
Inability to swallow or protect the airway
Cluster of cases suggesting a contaminated batch requiring public health action
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and ventilatory support through the critical period, recovery is usually complete within days; untreated severe cases can be fatal from respiratory failure, particularly where advanced support is unavailable.
pitfalls: Assuming thorough cooking removes the risk, as the toxins are heat-stable
Underestimating progression from paraesthesiae to respiratory failure
Mistaking preserved consciousness for a mild or non-organic presentation
Failing to notify public health authorities to prevent further poisonings
management: Supportive care centred on airway protection and mechanical ventilation through the period of respiratory-muscle paralysis, as there is no antidote
Early gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal, and gastric lavage, soon after ingestion once the airway is protected
Continuous respiratory monitoring with serial forced vital capacity and cardiac monitoring to anticipate ventilatory failure
Intravenous fluids and general intensive supportive care until toxin clearance
Careful neurological observation and reassurance, recognising that consciousness is preserved despite paralysis
Public health notification and identification of the implicated shellfish source to prevent further cases
